record_under_review.evidence_span: PuDGhost reveals that processing-using-DRAM operations based on simultaneous multiple-row activation can be corrupted by data in non-activated adjacent rows and by data in other columns computing concurrently. The study characterizes the phenomenon on 96 real DDR4 DRAM chips from 12 modules, finding up to 10% output impact from adjacent non-activated rows and up to 48% from concurrently computing columns for random inputs. It evaluates robust column screening and a compute-row layout with dedicated rows between compute rows as countermeasures on real chips.
record_under_review.hardware_or_process_assumptions: Real DDR4 DRAM using simultaneous multiple-row activation; results depend on chip organization, density, row layout, input patterns, and operating conditions.
record_under_review.limits: The evidence is an author preprint abstract; exact chip part numbers, voltage and temperature sweeps, full workload accuracy tables, screening cost, row-layout capacity cost, and transfer to other DRAM generations or PIM mechanisms require full-paper verification.
record_under_review.method_or_artifact: Empirical characterization of PuDGhost under simultaneous multiple-row activation, followed by cross-layer countermeasures including unreliable-column screening and compute-row layouts that separate active computation rows.
metrics: up to 10% output impact from adjacent non-activated rows
up to 48% output impact from concurrently computing columns
record_under_review.problem: Processing-using-DRAM assumes that each column's computation depends only on its own operands, but density scaling and neighboring-cell interference may violate that isolation and corrupt results.
record_under_review.title: PuDGhost: Experimental Analysis of Computation Result Corruption in Processing-using-DRAM Operations on Real DRAM Chips and Implications for Future Systems
record_under_review.workload_or_benchmark: Processing-using-DRAM operations on real DDR4 chips, including random-input experiments and computation-accuracy evaluation; the abstract identifies matrix-vector multiplication as a target workload context.
